newsitem.title: Japan: Japan PM sticks to guns on tax rise, pledges reform.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM sticks to guns on tax rise, pledges reform.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto stuck to his guns on tax rises and reiterated pledges of broad reform on Monday, but Tokyo financial markets signalled distaste for the former and deep doubts about the latter.
The Tokyo stock market, guessing accurately that Hashimoto would have little new to say when he addressed parliament on the first day of its new session, fell sharply from the start.

The key 225-share Nikkei average slid more than 800 points, discouraged by news that a sushi restaurant chain had collapsed with huge bad debts and hit by futures-linked selling. It then rebounded somewhat to close down 609.70 points at 17,480.34.
The share price plunge helped push the dollar to a 46-month high of 117.90 yen, partly on fears that the weak stock market would prompt foreign investors to ditch the Japanese currency.
"Not only voters, but financial markets are keenly interested in the session of parliament which opens on January 20," said an editorial in financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun.
"Many people are looking to the debate in parliament for clues as to whether or not the structural reform of Japan on the brink of the 21st century will proceed," the paper said.
A steep stock market decline that began late last year has boosted pressure on Hashimoto to rethink his budget, implement real reforms and ease fears about the economic future.
Officials, in response, have stressed that the outlook is less grim than the market fears.

Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita lent some support to that view on Monday, telling a central bank branch managers' meeting that Japan's economy was still gradually recovering and that the strength of the recovery was growing gradually.
Much of the recent market pessimism was sparked by Hashimoto's proposed tight budget for 1997/98, starting on April 1, which aims at getting Japan's big budget deficit under control.

Concern focused not only on fears that a higher tax burden could stall the recovery in its tracks, but also on the apparent lack of commitment to reform signalled by a failure to reject pleas to fund politicians' pet projects.

But Hashimoto on Monday confirmed he would forge ahead with a sales tax rise to five percent from three percent on April 1 and end two trillion yen ($17.0 billion) in special income tax cuts. He also warned of more belt-tightening in store.
"The 1997/98 budget is the first step towards fiscal reconstruction, and in future, more intense efforts are needed," he told parliament's Lower House.

Hashimoto also sounded his now-familiar refrain on other reforms, promising major -- but mostly unspecified -- changes in education, social security, the economic structure and the financial system, as well as to boost government efficiency.
Last November he announced a five-year "Big Bang" to liberalise Japan's financial markets, but details have yet to be worked out by various government panels.

Political analysts say Hashimoto's first big test will be whether his government can pass this year's extra budget by a self-imposed January 31 deadline and then pass -- without revision -- the budget for 1997/98 by the end of February to allow it to take effect even without Upper House approval.

Hashimoto may face some pressure from the two small parties which are partners in his loose ruling group to alter the 2.67 trillion yen ($22.8 billion) extra budget, but opposition parties look too weak to force major reforms to the 1997/98 budget, analysts say.

Hashimoto doubtless hopes to ride out a rough time in parliament and may well succeed -- barring a stock slump taking the Nikkei to 15,000, at which banks' hidden profits on shareholdings would evaporate and many would go into the red.
"His idea is to stiffen his resolve and rely on his near majority and opposition weakness to stick it out," said Jeff Young, a political analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia. ($1=117 yen)
